episode.title: 20VC: The Venture Model is Broken | You Need to be Greedy and Selfish to Win Early Stage Investing | Why Margins Do Not Matter for Early-Stage Startups | The Growth Rate that is Required in a World of AI with Gili Raanan, Founder @ Cyberstarts

highlights.speaker: Gili Raanan
highlights.text:
The venture business as a whole doesn't work. It shouldn't work. Returns and distribution are not divided equally between players — otherwise it would be too easy, there would be no winners and losers, and none of us would bother playing. So the expectation that venture as an asset class will work out is setting yourself up for disappointment from the start.

It has worked for some people, for some period of time. But the number of firms where it works consistently over a long period — your Sequoias, Andreessens, Benchmarks, Greylocks, Lightspeeds — is extremely small. Given the amount of money now flowing into venture, I don't think it's going to work for most. It's going to end up with serious catastrophe for many players.

If you're a limited partner who has distributed your venture allocation evenly across managers, you shouldn't sleep well at night. The math simply doesn't support it. In cybersecurity alone, roughly 350 to 400 new teams get funded every year, yet in Israel — which represents about 40% of the global market — only two companies became unicorns in 2025, and just one in 2024. The likelihood of hitting a successful company out of 150 new startups is still around 1%. And entry prices at seed are climbing from $15 million post-money a decade ago to $100 or $150 million today. The market is not balanced.

highlights.speaker: Gili Raanan
highlights.text:
We need to be selfish and we need to be greedy. Those are good traits for an early-stage investor — not negative traits at all. Price is an important consideration, and whenever I see an inflated seed deal that is essentially a bet on a team, I get more skeptical.

Venture is a game where we know very little when we get into investments. If we analyze product ideas and markets at the seed stage, mostly we are analyzing smoke, because founders will change their mind in a few weeks and it will be a different product, a different market, many different things. The outcome sizes in cybersecurity have indeed become massive — CrowdStrike and Palo Alto Networks have reached market caps that were never before thought possible. That's a legitimate argument for paying higher entry prices.

But it doesn't change the probability facts around this game. We should invest more in cybersecurity innovation, absolutely — the pain points are massive and real. But we should be super realistic as investors and limited partners about the ongoing and lasting impact of entry prices when we invest in emerging teams. The opportunity is here and it's real, but the discipline around what you pay still matters enormously.

highlights.speaker: Gili Raanan
highlights.text:
Trajectory, velocity, and growth rates are the most important indicators for a healthy business. Part of our job is to look at that growth and try to sense whether it's being engineered or organically achieved — there are ways to engineer growth. But whenever you see a business growing very fast, as a general statement, it's a good company, because that's the best predictor of future performance.

What I've learned over time is that when a business reaches a point where it's growing super fast, it becomes part of their DNA. It doesn't slow down just because of averages or mean reversion. There needs to be a significant external event to slow them down. At Wiz, the first quarter of selling software was a million dollars. Second quarter was two million. Then eight, then twenty-four. That's an amazing first year, in 2020. When you see that level of growth, it is not a one-time event.

Sierra had an amazing start too — half a million in the first quarter, then a million — and then they sold literally zero for two quarters. As an investor, you look at yourself and say, okay, I really messed up. But the founders analyzed what was happening, made modifications, and the next twelve months they sold twelve million in new business. It continued to grow extremely fast after that, because the thing that makes a company move fast typically does not simply fade away. It's baked into the organization.

highlights.speaker: Gili Raanan
highlights.text:
We are exercising the science of exceptions. The majority of companies do plateau — they hit twenty or thirty million and the markets just aren't as deep as expected, or they're more crowded. That's the rule. But the beauty of our profession is that it's made up of the exceptions, because who cares about the rules?

Take NoName, one of my Fund One portfolio companies focused on API security. They did about three million in the first year, fifteen million in the second — amazing growth. And then they slowed down. Why? API security wasn't really a market; it was a niche segment within application security. To sustain that growth, the company had to reinvent itself into a much bigger product and market vision, and it was super hard. We eventually sold the business to Akamai for about half a billion dollars.

Contrast that with Island, founded the same year, 2019. Their idea was the enterprise browser. In 2019, the number of CISOs who said they needed an enterprise browser was exactly zero — like the number of people in 2006 who said they needed an iPhone. The market didn't exist. And still, Island is a five-billion-dollar company today, growing very fast in a market it literally defined. They have tons of Fortune 100 customers, including major banks using an Island browser instead of Google or Microsoft — competing with free, which is extraordinarily difficult. These stories are instructive, but if you take them and apply them linearly, you'll struggle.

highlights.speaker: Gili Raanan
highlights.text:
I'm never worried about too much capital going into fast-growing companies and defocusing founders. It takes a lot of money to build those companies, and if we don't need the cash this year, we'll need it next year.

The real concern would be engineering growth with bad economics — if your magic number is horrible, and for every dollar you spend on sales and marketing you generate ten cents of new ARR, you're in a terrible business. You can throw money at it and your yield is so low you can never sustain it. But if you've built a product that fits what the market needs and you have a go-to-market team that executes well, your yield will be significantly higher. Maybe it's sixty-five cents on the dollar growing into eighty cents. You can see how it turns into a profitable business. Why would you care that you have an extra two hundred million in the bank?

The intellectual argument that a brilliant but young founder will bring forward a product roadmap, do four things instead of one, open geographies too soon, hire aggressively and poorly — I get it, but I don't buy it. I'm not in the business of babysitting founders. If we trust them to build a critical cybersecurity company that protects the most sensitive information of major U.S. banks, and then we tell them they can't handle having extra cushion in the bank without getting sloppy — that's not a bet I'd make.

highlights.speaker: Gili Raanan
highlights.text:
How often do I discuss gross margins with my early-stage companies? Never. My instincts tell me gross margins matter — the vital signs for a healthy cybersecurity company involve high, healthy gross margins. But part of our job as investors is to help founders realize what challenges they need to tackle right now versus what they should tackle in 2027 or 2028.

If you were a founder in the CyberStarts portfolio, I would tell you gross margins are important — let's talk about it in 2029. Let's build the foundations of a healthy business, assuming we will get to deal with gross margins eventually. We don't yet have enough examples of healthy, profitable AI businesses to really understand what the vital signs of a healthy AI company look like. Maybe AI is just a different margin profile we have to get used to.

The growth rate question is more interesting. Exceptional companies have traditionally grown at an extremely high pace. My benchmark for the first five years after you start selling is 4X, 4X, 3X, 3X on new ARR — not total ARR, but new ARR each year. That's 144X after five years. If you booked a million in year one, you're booking 144 million in year five. I don't think there's a limit on what great looks like, and five years from now someone will make Wiz look like a slug. But the bar for real greatness pretty much stays the same.

highlights.speaker: Gili Raanan
highlights.text:
Going public is not a financial event. It's a branding event. It's an occasion where you tell your customers, your partners, your employees, and your future employees: I'm here to stay. Typically it's the opposite of a liquidity event — you get shackles on your hands, you can't sell stock, you've got all kinds of limitations. It's hell for liquidity, but it's an important marketing event.

I believe many founders and companies will still choose to go through that exercise and pay the price of reduced flexibility and liquidity to gain the long-term value of that marketing event. But the extension of private markets that we're seeing — where companies like Stripe and Canva stay private — is functional and sustainable.

The key issue with extended private timelines is talent retention. You typically grant employees stock for four, maybe five years. After they're fully vested, you're structurally unable to allocate equally large or tempting grants because the company is bigger with more employees. Your best engineers, product managers, and salespeople are fully vested, most of their family wealth is tied to one company, and it's perfectly logical for them to consider diversification by joining another startup. The antidote is secondaries — recurring liquidity programs, not one-off deals. At CyberStarts, we created an employee liquidity fund that underwrites a tender offer every year so employees get the same kind of liquidity they'd have at a public company.

highlights.speaker: Gili Raanan
highlights.text:
Early on at CyberStarts, I thought it was a good thing to show our limited partners that we could drive liquidity from our incredible paper portfolio. We sold secondary shares in companies like Wiz. I regret selling every single share — if I had sold later, I would have shown better performance for my LPs. But at the time it looked like the right and responsible thing to do.

There's a potential misalignment between GPs and LPs here. An early GP will want to distribute and show great DPI because they want to raise a bigger fund sooner. But if you're a long-hold LP, you might want the GP to retain the position. It's always easier to see this in hindsight. When I made the decision, the reaction from my sophisticated LPs was overwhelmingly positive — they were cheering because for them it was a new GP and distributions were a positive signal. I had only one or two super smart LPs who pushed back. One called and said, 'I'm not investing here to hedge my risks. I actually want to take more risks.'

Secondaries make markets more sophisticated. With that sophistication you can create better solutions for employees, founders, and limited partners. It's a highly positive element in the business overall. But the lesson for me was personal — I learned that the instinct to prove yourself as a new manager can cost you if the underlying asset is truly exceptional.

highlights.speaker: Gili Raanan
highlights.text:
Venture is a terrible profession in one specific sense: you don't know if you're good at what you're doing for five or six years. Show me another profession where you show up to work every day for five years and have no idea if you're doing any good. In that sense, it's genuinely terrible.

When I was at Sequoia Capital, I'd show up to the office surrounded by super achievers building amazing companies. I'd look in the mirror and say, I'm the worst investor in this room. There are ten people around me and I'm the worst. The next day, same thing. It's really hard. You have really bad days. It takes a lot of greed and determination to keep going and believe you're going to figure it out. My hardest day as an investor was when the first company I invested in had to shut down — a very public failure you can't cover or explain away.

But I think it's one of the most exciting professions in the world because it gives you the opportunity to share your life with so many amazing individuals. The only constant is the diversity and change of the people you meet and partner with. You gain a little bit from every team, and cumulatively you gain a lot. You have to become a better listener over time, and that by itself makes you a better person, a better parent, a better partner. It's not a one-time change — it's a gradual transformation, and the more teams you go on the journey with, the better version of yourself you become.

highlights.speaker: Gili Raanan
highlights.text:
One non-trivial lesson I've learned about building a venture partnership is that people are very different and they bring different talents. As a managing partner, a very easy mistake is to try to create guardrails and a textbook and bring everyone into the same mode of operation. You do that because you think, this is what worked for me — now let me map the gaps between how this new partner performs and my recipe, and bridge the gap.

My view now is the opposite: let each team member play to their relative strengths. Don't require them to focus on improving their weaknesses. On their weaknesses, at best they'll be as good as the market average. But on the things where they're exceptional, they create real advantage, real greatness.

That leaves CyberStarts with a team of people who genuinely enjoy working with each other, but each of us operates differently, and we respect that. I learned this through mistakes — I put guardrails on people before, constrained them to my way of thinking, and realized it was a net negative for them even though it had been a positive for me. The team gets stronger when you let people be spiky rather than well-rounded.

highlights.speaker: Gili Raanan
highlights.text:
I focus on the deals I've done and the teams I've partnered with. That's where I put my focus and energy. You can't cover everything and you can't get everything. You are not going to win every battle, and if you are stressed about winning every battle — 'I need to be in every important AI company,' 'I need to be in every important cybersecurity company' — I can predict that you're not going to succeed at that.

Have I lost deals in the last five years? Yes. Could I have done more? Absolutely. There are always things you could do — another customer call, another intro, hire someone for the founder, pay more. We are improving the CyberStarts business all the time. I tell my partners constantly that we are always only as good as our next investment.

But it really doesn't matter, because if all our investments are amazing and we lost one or two companies, that doesn't change the outcome. Everything leads me to the same conclusion: focus on your own thing. We typically get what we want to get. We can always improve. And I'm very happy with the progress. The one thing I've changed my mind on most recently is how important founder chemistry is. Focus on the teams you have the most chemistry with. And test it simply: do the founders know each other? Were they roommates? Did they work together through real challenges? The founding relationship matters extremely.

highlights.speaker: Gili Raanan
highlights.text:
Public market multipliers are just the market's anticipation of your growth rate. If the market believes a company's growth rate will decline — perhaps because autonomous AI programs might eat part of its business — you'll see the multiplier drop. But if those companies continue to grow at an incredible pace regardless of market sentiment, the multipliers will rebound.

I'm confused and baffled by public markets, honestly. You have Monday trading at one and a half times revenue, Wix at two and a half times. These are real businesses. My guess is there's an expectation that AI will displace some of their value, but I'm not confident in that explanation.

What I am confident about is the relationship between growth and valuation. The multiplier is a forward-looking growth indicator, nothing more. If you're an investor looking at your portfolio turning red, the question isn't whether the multiples are fair — it's whether the underlying growth engines of those businesses are intact. If they are, patience will be rewarded. If the market is right that growth is decelerating, then the repricing is rational. Either way, the answer comes back to the same thing: growth rate is what matters most.

episode.title: Uncapped #45 | Ron Conway from SV Angel

highlights.speaker: Ron Conway
highlights.text:
Conway's career traces a through-line across every major technology cycle — semiconductors, PCs, software, the internet, and now AI. He started at National Semiconductor when Santa Clara Valley was still fruit orchards, then joined a breakout called Altos Computer as head of sales, sitting next to the copy machine in a office with no desks. Altos went public successfully in the mid-1980s, but complacency set in and the company was disrupted by PCs connected to Ethernet — a lesson Conway distills into a core principle: if you don't disrupt yourself, you will be disrupted.

After selling Altos to Acer, Conway found himself at loose ends. Don Valentine, the founder of Sequoia Capital and Altos's lead board member, suggested he sit in on board meetings and try angel investing. Conway sat in on his first board meeting and was spellbound — Valentine was giving founders advice that Conway knew he could give himself. That moment launched a career in angel investing that would eventually touch Google, Facebook, Stripe, Airbnb, and dozens of other defining companies.

What's striking is that Conway's very first angel investment was a company called Natural Language Incorporated, a Berkeley AI startup — decades before the current boom. The company ran out of payroll and Conway brokered a rapid acquisition by Microsoft, refusing to let Bill Gates delay the deal even a single day. The investment that really got the flywheel spinning, though, was Ask Jeeves, which Conway built alongside Ben Rosen, the legendary Morgan Stanley analyst. The two would ride together to board meetings that were really company-building sessions, and Conway describes that period as some of the most fun he's ever had in his career.

highlights.speaker: Ron Conway
highlights.text:
Conway draws a sharp distinction between angel investing as most people imagine it — passive, check-writing, wait-and-see — and the way SV Angel actually operates. His firm's unofficial moniker is 'advocates for founders,' and the approach is holistic: they want to help the whole person, not just the business. That means career development, team building, and showing up for problems that have nothing to do with cap tables or product strategy.

The examples Conway gives are remarkably personal. He describes getting calls from founders whose parents have been diagnosed with serious illness, and immediately activating a deep relationship with UCSF's department heads to get them the best possible care. He recounts being woken up in Venice in the middle of the night to arrange top-tier neurological care for a prominent figure in the valley, and refusing to accept anything less than the head of neurology as the attending physician.

This isn't performative generosity — it's a philosophy that the best investor-founder relationships are built on trust forged in moments of genuine crisis. When a founder knows their investor will pick up the phone at 2 AM to help with a family emergency, the professional relationship transforms into something far more durable and productive.

highlights.speaker: Ron Conway
highlights.text:
The relationship network Conway has built over four decades is, in his own assessment, SV Angel's most valuable asset — more important than any individual investment thesis. It started organically at National Semiconductor, where Steve Jobs came recruiting executives for Apple. Conway ended up with connections to Apple's early leadership simply because they came from his semiconductor world. Then as he moved into software and then internet companies, each generation of executives carried relationships from the prior era forward.

Marc Andreessen calls Conway 'the human router,' and Conway takes it as a compliment. He describes a constant background process running in his head: whenever he meets someone, he's thinking about who else they should know. He connects people with no expectation of immediate return, but he does keep track of the significant introductions. He recounts a recent conversation where someone was bragging about a deal, and Conway quietly pointed out that he had made the original introduction that set the whole thing in motion.

The compounding effect is powerful. Investing in defining companies like Google, Twitter, and Meta — and helping build their management teams — created a web of relationships that subsequent founders could tap into. A call to a senior executive at one of these companies to set up a distribution deal for a portfolio company is easy when you helped hire that executive in the first place. It's a flywheel that has been spinning for forty years.

highlights.speaker: Ron Conway
highlights.text:
Conway believes that being an effective relationship broker requires a genuine personality trait: you have to love meeting new people. He estimates that maybe forty percent of people are simply not wired for it — they're shy, uninterested, or drained by constant social interaction. His wife, he notes, hates meeting new people. But for Conway, gathering people and connecting them is energizing, not depleting.

The key insight is that this can't be faked or done transactionally. Conway describes deliberately building relationships with people in government, media, and Hollywood — not because he had an immediate need, but because he knew that eventually someone in his portfolio would. He was exploring Hollywood connections as early as 1988, through Shaquille O'Neal's agent Len Armato, who was convinced streaming was about to explode. They invested in audio and video companies 'way too early,' but the relationships endured.

This premeditated but non-transactional approach extends to government as well. Conway has made it his business to always know the two state senators, the governor, and key congressional leaders. The relationships are built over years of genuine engagement, not crisis-driven phone calls. When a founder runs into a regulatory problem, Conway already has the relationship capital to make the call — because he's been showing up long before he needed anything.

highlights.speaker: Ron Conway
highlights.text:
Conway's approach to inflection points reveals what separates a great angel investor from a good one. SV Angel explicitly tells founders: we're not going to hover or look over your shoulder, but when you hit a life-or-death moment, that's where we excel. The firm mobilizes completely in those moments, setting everything else aside.

The Airbnb COVID story is a dramatic illustration. When the pandemic hit, Brian Chesky's board was questioning whether the company could survive. Conway's response was immediate and forceful: 'You bet your ass we have a company.' He told the three co-founders to call him at any hour, then delivered a lecture about who was actually in charge of their destiny. The board had told them fundraising was impossible — there was COVID, nobody would invest. Conway ignored that advice, and within ten days had raised hundreds of millions from Silver Lake through a creative instrument.

The pattern repeats across crises. Conway doesn't wait to be asked, doesn't hedge, and doesn't defer to conventional wisdom. He assesses the situation with his own conviction and acts. The founders are smart enough to know what needs to happen — Chesky already knew he'd need to lay off half the company — but what they need in those moments is someone with conviction, relationships, and the willingness to fight on their behalf.

highlights.speaker: Ron Conway
highlights.text:
The Silicon Valley Bank collapse in March 2023 may have been Conway's most consequential intervention. The crisis hit on the day of SV Angel's annual founders summit, and Conway didn't sleep for three days. The core problem was straightforward — the FDIC needed to guarantee deposits — but the bureaucratic and political machinery wasn't moving fast enough.

Conway discovered that the FDIC reports only to Congress, not to the executive branch, which meant the levers of power ran through specific committee chairs: Sherrod Brown in the Senate and Maxine Waters in the House. By Sunday morning, with roughly six hours before the Tokyo stock market opened and a potential worldwide financial crisis, Conway got very firm with the people who could authorize the guarantee. His message was blunt: you're going to be responsible for a global meltdown if you don't act now.

Wally Adeyamo, the Deputy Secretary of Treasury under Janet Yellen, later told Conway at dinner that he didn't fully appreciate how close things had come or how pivotal Conway's aggressive intervention had been. Conway's reflection on the episode is characteristically direct: you have to have conviction, know how to navigate the system, and be willing to make people uncomfortable. His proposed gravestone inscription — 'fearless for founders' — captures the philosophy perfectly.

highlights.speaker: Ron Conway
highlights.text:
When Sam Altman was briefly ousted from OpenAI, Conway treated it as a case of a founder being mistreated and mobilized accordingly. He had conviction that the situation was wrong and set about making it right, taking no prisoners. Conway frames this kind of intervention not as optional or heroic but as a core obligation of an investor who claims to be an advocate for founders.

Conway acknowledges that Silicon Valley probably doesn't have enough of this kind of toughness. Many companies go out of business, he says, because nobody was willing to fight for them at the critical moment. Other industries — finance, media, politics — tend to produce people who are more comfortable with confrontation. Tech culture, for all its rhetoric about disruption, can be surprisingly passive when it comes to political and institutional battles.

The willingness to fight requires a specific psychological makeup. Conway names three elements: being genuinely competitive and hating to lose, being comfortable with people being angry at you, and being fearless on behalf of the people you're fighting for. He notes that his decades of experience have given him an additional tool — the ability to call someone and simply ask, 'Do you want to do this the hard way or the easy way?' That kind of credible threat only works when backed by a long track record of following through.

highlights.speaker: Ron Conway
highlights.text:
SV Angel has always been a thematic investor, organizing its portfolio around six or so themes at any given time. In the early days, Conway watched Yahoo, Ask Jeeves, and Lycos and concluded that something big was happening in search — so search became a theme. B2B became another. Any company that walked in the door fitting one of those themes got a serious look; companies that didn't fit were turned down quickly.

This thematic discipline serves as both a filter and a conviction engine. Rather than trying to evaluate every possible startup on its individual merits, Conway builds a thesis about where technology is heading and then looks for the best teams executing within that thesis. Today, of course, everything is AI — but even within AI, SV Angel maintains sub-themes to create structure and focus.

The approach naturally produces a diversified portfolio with occasional massive winners, which is the mathematical reality of seed investing. Conway doesn't frame it in terms of portfolio theory or power laws — he frames it in terms of intellectual curiosity. He invests in what's interesting, and the themes reflect what he and his team believe is about to explode. The returns follow from getting the themes right and then being the kind of investor that the best founders within those themes want to work with.

highlights.speaker: Ron Conway
highlights.text:
Conway has been politically engaged on behalf of the tech industry since its earliest regulatory fights. He recounts the SOPA/PIPA battle, when media companies tried to outlaw internet-distributed content. A seasoned lobbyist told Conway — then a self-described rookie at political activism — to literally go stand on a soapbox outside city hall and make a speech. Conway felt foolish doing it, but the cameras were rolling, and it helped turn the tide.

The Napster connection proved useful in that fight. SV Angel was an early investor in Napster, and Sean Fanning happened to be with Senator Orrin Hatch when Conway needed a congressional ally. Conway told Fanning to drop whatever he was talking about and pitch the senator on opposing the legislation. Hatch became the first senator to publicly vote against SOPA.

Conway's broader philosophy is that the tech industry must be civically engaged as a matter of course, not just when a crisis arrives. Companies should know their local politicians, contribute to civic life, and build relationships with legislators based on job creation — a message that resonates across party lines. The relationship has to be genuine and long-standing; showing up only when you need something is the surest way to be ignored.

highlights.speaker: Ron Conway
highlights.text:
Conway is sounding the alarm about a proposed California ballot initiative that would impose a 5% annual wealth tax on every asset — real estate, art, cars, financial holdings. The initiative is being driven by a single healthcare workers' union, and if it collects 900,000 signatures, it goes before voters. What makes the proposal especially destructive, in Conway's view, is a provision that taxes founders based on their voting control rather than their actual ownership stake.

The practical consequence is stark: if a founder like Larry Page or Sergey Brin owns 10% of a company's shares but holds 80% voting control, the tax would be assessed on 80% of the market capitalization. Conway argues this is why certain high-profile founders have already left California — it wasn't a lifestyle choice but a financial necessity. The provision effectively penalizes the dual-class share structures that many tech founders use to maintain long-term strategic control of their companies.

The strategy Conway is pursuing involves keeping the measure off the ballot entirely, rather than fighting it at the polls where populist wealth-tax messaging could prevail. He's working with Governor Newsom to negotiate with the union, and notes that other labor unions — including the teachers' union — are furious at the healthcare union for pursuing this alone. Counter ballot initiatives are being organized to give Newsom additional bargaining leverage. Conway frames this as another case of recognizing the problem, building conviction, and going to fight — the same pattern that has defined his career.

highlights.speaker: Ron Conway
highlights.text:
Conway's philosophy of corporate culture traces back to his experience at Altos Computer, where Don Valentine chose to join the board specifically because he admired the company's culture. The motto was 'play hard, work hard' — there was alcohol on Friday nights, but Monday morning everyone was back at it. Dave Jackson's kids worked there. It was, by Conway's account, a genuinely fun and ethical place.

Valentine's lesson stuck: culture is something a founder has to deliberately build, and bad culture — Conway pointedly mentions companies that 'allow philandering' — produces companies where leaders are not role models. He extends this philosophy to SV Angel's portfolio companies today, insisting that founders should also be philanthropically engaged. The byproduct, he argues, isn't just good PR — it's that company morale genuinely explodes when employees feel their work has a purpose beyond revenue.

This cultural sensibility runs through everything Conway does. SV Angel encourages founders to be civically engaged, to build relationships with local politicians, and to think of themselves as part of a broader tech ecosystem rather than isolated operators. The firm practices what it preaches: Conway's three sons all independently chose to join the investing world after sitting in on SV Angel's weekly meetings, and they all operate out of the same office. The family dynamic mirrors the company-building ethos Conway has advocated for decades.

episode.title: Submarines and the Future of Defense Manufacturing

highlights.speaker: Vice Admiral Robert Goucher
highlights.text:
The real advantage that submarines bring is stealth and access — the ability to go virtually anywhere in the world undetected. That capability underpins two critical missions. Fast attack submarines keep global sea lanes free and open, ensuring that allies like Australia can receive the supplies they depend on even when adversaries try to shut trade routes down.

The higher-priority mission is strategic deterrence. Ballistic missile submarines like the Columbia class carry nuclear weapons and, because they cannot be found, guarantee a second-strike capability. Any nation that launched a nuclear attack on the United States would face assured destruction from submarines already at sea. That is why they are called the survivable leg of the nuclear triad.

This dynamic has preserved decades of peace without nuclear war. Deterrence works precisely because potential adversaries know the submarines are out there and that retaliation is inevitable. The entire architecture of global nuclear stability rests on the assumption that these boats remain hidden, armed, and ready.

highlights.speaker: Chris Power
highlights.text:
At the end of the Cold War, the United States effectively walked away from submarine manufacturing. Through the entire 1990s, only about three submarines were built. Even when production resumed with the Virginia class at a rate of one per year, that required roughly 13 million labor hours per boat. Today the Navy needs to build two Virginias plus one Columbia annually — a workload on the order of 70 million hours, more than five times the capacity of just a decade ago.

The bottleneck is not money. The capital can be raised and spent. What vanished was the skilled workforce. Nine out of ten manufacturing jobs disappeared after the Cold War, and an entire generation was told to skip the trades and pursue four-year degrees instead. The machinists, welders, and quality inspectors who remained are now in their late fifties and sixties, and nobody replaced them.

The only viable path is a productivity leap that fuses software with a new workforce. You cannot hire two million welders who do not exist. Advanced factories have to make each worker dramatically more productive — augmenting skills with software, compressing training timelines, and running facilities around the clock with machine assistance. That is the core challenge: not a budget gap, but a people gap that technology must close.

highlights.speaker: Vice Admiral Robert Goucher
highlights.text:
The role of direct-reporting portfolio manager for submarines — colloquially, the submarine czar — was created because the Deputy Secretary of Defense wanted to eliminate bureaucratic friction on the programs most critical to strategic deterrence. Three such roles were established: one for Golden Dome missile defense, one for the Air Force's bomber and ICBM programs, and one for submarines.

The logic is straightforward. When authority is concentrated in a single accountable person who reports directly to the deputy secretary, layers of coordination that would normally slow decisions can be short-circuited. Instead of twenty stakeholders each contributing a piece, one person has the mandate to make fast decisions, take calculated risks, and place multiple bets simultaneously.

Success over the next three to five years means being on cadence to deliver the submarines the Navy needs. The fleet may not hit full production rate in three years, but every lever — outsourced manufacturing, workforce development, supply chain expansion — must be moving in the right direction. The transition is still early, but the structural change is designed to ensure that progress is measured by outcomes, not process compliance.

highlights.speaker: Chris Power
highlights.text:
A submarine is not like a Toyota Camry, where you set up a production line and crank out twenty thousand identical units a year. Submarine manufacturing is high-mix, low-volume — you might need one of a particular component and then a slight variant, and you often do not know exactly when you will need it. Traditional factory automation, the kind that works for iPhones or cars, simply does not apply.

What software enables is running at the productivity level of a highly automated factory while retaining the flexibility that submarine construction demands. Lines can be reconfigured on demand to produce whatever the shipyards need at that moment. Without that capability, a single missing part can stall an entire construction sequence — and going back to the supply chain for that part might take twelve months.

This combination of velocity, agility, and reduced labor requirements is what makes a modern software-driven factory fundamentally different from a traditional one. It is not about eliminating people. It is about making each person dramatically more effective and making the production system responsive enough to handle the inherent unpredictability of building one of the most complex machines ever engineered.

highlights.speaker: Vice Admiral Robert Goucher
highlights.text:
Building a submarine requires three things: people, productivity, and parts. On productivity, some areas of submarine construction today operate at less than fifty percent efficiency — for every two workers, you get one effective labor hour. That is not anyone's fault; it reflects where the workforce is after decades of attrition. Even at the peak of the mid-1980s, when the country was producing four nuclear submarines a year, productivity only reached about 0.7 or 0.8. There is a ceiling on what a human alone can achieve.

Machines change that equation. They can run around the clock and execute certain tasks more effectively than manual labor. The productivity uplift from combining skilled workers with advanced manufacturing tools and software is not incremental — it is the difference between meeting production targets and falling short.

On parts, the single biggest thing that stops work in the shipyards is what is called sequence-critical material: you reach a step in construction that requires one specific component, and if it is not there, everything halts. Having flexible manufacturing capacity that can produce those parts on demand — air flasks, escape trunk hatches, obsolete components from suppliers that went out of business — is where facilities like Hadrian's can have an immediate and outsized impact.

highlights.speaker: Vice Admiral Robert Goucher
highlights.text:
One of the most promising early opportunities for new manufacturing capacity is supporting in-service submarines — boats that have already been built but need periodic maintenance, pump repairs, or valve replacements. Many of the original suppliers for those parts have gone out of business, leaving the Navy with obsolete components and no source.

Turning those obsolete parts over to an advanced manufacturer that can reverse-engineer and produce them means keeping the existing fleet operational while new construction ramps up. It is a concrete, near-term win that does not require waiting years for full qualification on new-build components.

This kind of sustainment work also serves as a proving ground. As facilities demonstrate capability on maintenance parts and first articles, they build the track record and qualification history needed to take on increasingly complex new-build work for the Virginia and Columbia programs.

highlights.speaker: Vice Admiral Robert Goucher
highlights.text:
Submarines will remain relevant as long as the force keeps thinking forward and pacing adversaries. The ability to get off another country's coast undetected and choose what to deploy — missiles, torpedoes, or increasingly, underwater drones — gives the platform extraordinary flexibility. The key insight is that payloads can be built outside the submarine and loaded on as needed, so whatever the conflict of the future demands, the platform can adapt.

Because submarines are self-sustaining with their own defense and command-and-control capability, they can also serve as forward nodes in a larger network. A submarine could connect with a constellation of drones, provide the signal and human-in-the-loop decision-making, and coordinate operations without ever firing a weapon itself.

This evolution from a weapons platform to a command-and-control hub for autonomous systems is where manned and unmanned capabilities converge. The submarine provides the stealth, the endurance, and the human judgment; the drones provide scale and expendability. Together they create a force structure that is far more capable than either component alone.

highlights.speaker: Chris Power
highlights.text:
The biggest misconception about modern defense manufacturing is that it is all automated and does not need people. The reality is the opposite. Standing up an advanced factory requires enormous numbers of software engineers and experienced manufacturing talent from companies like Tesla, SpaceX, and GE. Workforce development has to be a national mission, not an afterthought.

People also underestimate the sheer difficulty of submarine construction. In terms of tolerancing, precision, quality, and welding requirements, submarines are arguably the most demanding manufacturing challenge in existence — more difficult than building rockets. Every component must function flawlessly for thirty to forty years underwater, with lives depending on it.

Doing this kind of work outside the traditional private shipyards or the Navy itself, and successfully transferring that institutional knowledge to a new facility, is unprecedented. It is not just about making parts. It is about achieving a level of precision and quality assurance that has historically existed in only a handful of places in the country, and proving that it can be replicated and scaled.

highlights.speaker: Chris Power
highlights.text:
Three years ago, working with the government on something of this scale was incredibly difficult. What has changed is that Congress, the Navy, and the Department of Defense have collectively hit the accelerate button and removed many of the structural blockers. For a project of this size and complexity, moving from concept to a 2.25-million-square-foot factory opening in six or seven months is remarkably fast — comparable to or faster than what the commercial sector could achieve.

The most important structural change is cultural: establishing single accountable leaders instead of governance by committee. When one person has command and control over an entire enterprise — whether submarines, drone dominance, or missile defense — they can make fast decisions and place multiple bets simultaneously. That is not possible when twenty people all need to contribute to every decision.

This same principle applies to Hadrian's approach. The company has structured itself so that its incentives are fully aligned with the Navy's outcomes — capital is at risk, meaning the team cannot succeed unless the Navy succeeds. That alignment, combined with the mission imperative, creates a culture where people will push relentlessly until the job is done.

highlights.speaker: Vice Admiral Robert Goucher
highlights.text:
The experience that companies building small autonomous underwater vehicles and drones gain from constructing integrated systems has genuine corollaries to submarine manufacturing. Building an unmanned vessel still requires integrating sensors, propulsion, communications, and control systems into a functioning whole, and those skills can translate to building modules for full-scale submarines.

But there is an important distinction. Drone capabilities are typically single-mission systems — they do one thing and are often designed to be expendable. A submarine with a human crew is a multi-mission platform: responsive, versatile, and capable of adapting to any number of situations in real time. It is not a niche tool but a general-purpose instrument of national power.

The future likely involves both. Large manned submarines serve as command-and-control hubs and multi-mission platforms, while smaller autonomous systems extend their reach and handle tasks where expendability is acceptable. The manufacturing ecosystem that supports both — from advanced factories producing precision submarine components to agile lines building drones at scale — is what the country needs to build.

highlights.speaker: Chris Power
highlights.text:
Training a Navy welder today takes roughly a decade. The country does not have a decade to wait for each new worker, nor does it have the existing workforce to draw from. The solution is a two-part approach: augment existing skills with software to make workers dramatically more productive, and simultaneously make training far more accessible so new people can contribute meaningfully much sooner.

At the task level, the goal is to make each worker ninety percent more productive and reduce the cognitive burden of the remaining human-in-the-loop work. If you translate the seventy million labor hours the Navy needs into a people requirement and then apply software-driven productivity gains, you can cut the workforce needed by fifty to seventy percent. That is the difference between an achievable goal and an impossible one.

This is fundamentally about the productivity-per-person equation. The workers who built submarines in the 1980s spent careers accumulating knowledge that let them operate at peak efficiency. Software can encode much of that institutional knowledge — tolerances, sequencing, quality checks — and deliver it to a newer, less experienced workforce in a form they can act on immediately. The goal is not to replace the human but to compress what used to take a generation of apprenticeship into something the country can actually scale.

episode.title: Investor Stories 468: Selling Too Early, LP Pressure, and Investor Tension — Lessons from Investors at Foundry Group, Centana Growth, and Andreessen Horowitz (Levine, Byunn, Ulevitch)

highlights.speaker: Seth Levine
highlights.text:
Misalignment around when and how to sell a company is one of the most common conflicts in venture capital. It can surface between investors and management — where one side wants to keep building and the other sees an attractive exit — or among investors themselves. The disagreements often trace back to structural differences: one investor got in at a lower basis and needs a bigger outcome to move the needle, or someone is in the middle of fundraising and desperately wants to show DPI to their LPs.

The root problem is rarely the disagreement itself — it's the refusal to name what's actually driving it. Early in my career I watched people argue passionately for a position while refusing to admit the real motivation. Someone would push to sell and never say 'I'm fundraising right now and I need distributions.' A CEO would advocate for an exit without saying 'My kids are 12 and 13 and I want some financial security.' When the true motivation stays hidden, the group can't solve the actual problem.

If you know a co-investor needs liquidity, maybe you can structure a partial sale or secondary. If the CEO wants personal financial security, maybe there's a way to let them take some chips off the table without selling the whole company. But none of those creative solutions are available if everyone is pretending their position is purely about the business. The fix is radical transparency about biases and incentives — not more sophisticated arguments.

highlights.speaker: Eric Byunn
highlights.text:
The highest-stakes conflict in venture capital, repeatedly, is the question of when to exit a company. Management teams can land on either side — some want to keep building, others feel they've achieved success and are ready to move on. Investors take different positions too, often shaped by when they entered and at what terms. And unfortunately, some investors behave unethically around the exit question, which escalates conflict dramatically.

Despite the intensity these disputes can reach, two principles reliably govern how they get resolved. First, it is nearly impossible to reach a good outcome without alignment with the management team. You can try to persuade, you can apply pressure, but nine times out of ten, management effectively wins the debate. When the dispute is among investors rather than with management, the NVCA legal documents provide clear voting mechanisms, and formal votes are how those disagreements get settled.

When it comes to taking a secondary exit — say a new round investor offers to buy you out at some multiple — the first filter is whether the founder and management team support it. If they're opposed, that should be the end of the conversation. If they're supportive, it becomes a portfolio management decision grounded in fiduciary duty. Venture investors manage capital on behalf of nonprofits, educational institutions, and pension funds, and the decision must be evaluated from those beneficiaries' perspective, not the investor's personal preference.

highlights.speaker: David Ulevitch
highlights.text:
One of the most disorienting conflicts in venture is discovering that a firm you regularly co-invest with has a serious grievance against you — and you had no idea. It's like finding out a close friend has quietly resented you for months. The conflict surfaced during a deal where both firms were trying to invest in the same company, and suddenly the founders were caught in the middle of a fight they didn't create.

What started as a surprise escalated quickly. Initial phone calls involved yelling and real anger. The grievances turned out to be largely philosophical — disagreements about how the firms build and operate, not about any single transaction. Resolving it took about two months of sustained conversation, pulling in senior partners on both sides and leaning hard on relationships built over years. The pitch was simple: we can go to war and eventually it spills out publicly, or we can acknowledge we have different philosophies while recognizing that when it comes to supporting entrepreneurs and building companies, we're deeply aligned.

Everyone ultimately recognized that great companies would keep emerging in overlapping categories, and both firms would want to be co-investors. The rational path was cooperation. But the episode was genuinely stressful — especially the fear of being the partner creating drama for your own firm. The optimistic side of venture gets most of the airtime, but the reality is that every week brings a different difficult challenge. It's the underbelly of the business, unglamorous but unavoidable.

highlights.speaker: David Ulevitch
highlights.text:
When Andreessen Horowitz launched American Dynamism and began investing in defense companies — many with offensive capabilities — the LP base pushed back hard. The early days were filled with emails and questions, many of them hypothetical scenarios that bordered on absurd. LPs were testing the boundaries of what the fund would back and trying to understand where the ethical lines were drawn.

The resolution wasn't a single conversation but a sustained education campaign. The firm spent significant time walking LPs through why defense technology was exciting, why it was strategically important, and crucially, why they believed it would generate strong financial returns. The financial case matters because LPs are themselves fiduciaries — they need to justify their allocations to their own stakeholders.

That tension has largely dissipated now, but it illustrates a broader dynamic: LPs and GPs don't always share the same instincts about what constitutes an appropriate investment. When a fund pushes into a new or controversial category, the GP has to earn that mandate through patient persuasion, not just assert it through the fund documents.

highlights.speaker: Seth Levine
highlights.text:
There's a particular move in boardroom disagreements where investors argue forcefully for a position while carefully concealing the real reason behind it. The stated rationale sounds strategic — market timing, competitive dynamics, valuation framework — but the actual driver is something personal and structural. They're raising a new fund and need distributions to show prospective LPs. Their fund is approaching end of life and they need to return capital. They got in at a high basis and this exit doesn't clear their threshold.

Calling this out directly is uncomfortable, and most people avoid it. But avoiding it means the group optimizes against a phantom problem while the real one festers. If an investor needs DPI for fundraising, that's a solvable problem — maybe through a secondary sale of their position, or a structured partial liquidity event. If a CEO wants financial security for their family, you can explore personal liquidity without forcing a full company sale. The solution space opens up dramatically once the actual constraint is on the table.

Bluntness in these moments isn't about being confrontational for its own sake. It's about efficiency. The sooner everyone's real incentives are visible, the sooner the group can find a path that works for the most stakeholders. The worst outcomes happen when people let unstated motivations drive major decisions about a company's future.

highlights.speaker: Eric Byunn
highlights.text:
The question of founder alignment isn't just a nice philosophical stance — it's a practical necessity baked into how venture deals actually work. Most governance structures give founders and management significant control over exit decisions. Even when investors technically have the votes to force an outcome, trying to push through a sale or exit over management's objections almost never produces a good result. The management team controls execution, customer relationships, and institutional knowledge. An unwilling management team going through a forced acquisition is a recipe for value destruction.

This is why the 'founder friendly' label, when it's real and not just marketing, translates into a concrete decision rule: if the founder and management team are against an exit, you don't pursue it. Full stop. That principle was tested in situations where secondary buyers offered attractive multiples, and the discipline held. The logic is straightforward — you entered the investment alongside these people, your interests should remain aligned throughout.

When management is supportive of an exit, the calculus shifts to pure portfolio management. At that point, investors need to think like the fiduciaries they are, evaluating the offer against the risk-adjusted future value of the position, and making that judgment on behalf of the pensions, endowments, and nonprofits whose capital they deploy.

highlights.speaker: David Ulevitch
highlights.text:
The instinct when you discover an inter-firm conflict is to minimize it — to assume it's minor and will resolve itself. That instinct is almost always wrong. What seemed like a small philosophical disagreement turned out to be deep-seated resentment that had been building quietly over multiple deals and interactions. The other firm had cataloged grievances that individually might have been small but collectively amounted to a fundamental problem with how the relationship was functioning.

The resolution required something that venture capitalists aren't always comfortable with: sustained vulnerability. Rather than posturing or lawyering up, the approach was to pull in senior partners who had long-standing personal relationships with the other firm and have honest conversations about what went wrong. The framing that ultimately worked wasn't 'who's right' but 'what serves the founders we both want to back.' That shared mission provided enough common ground to rebuild the working relationship.

The episode also surfaced an internal fear that's rarely discussed — the anxiety of being the partner who brings drama to your own firm. Venture partnerships depend on trust and low friction among partners. When your external relationships create internal stress, it threatens your standing in your own house. That double pressure — needing to resolve the external conflict while managing the internal perception — made the situation significantly more stressful than a straightforward business negotiation.
